subject: Chemistry
title: Strychnine: Rat Poison Turned Murder Weapon
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Strychnine: Rat Poison Turned Murder Weapon.

hook.text: Strychnine causes one of the most horrifying deaths in toxicology—violent, uncontrollable muscle spasms.

buildup.text: It comes from the seeds of the Strychnos nux-vomica tree. Just 30 mg can kill an adult.

discovery.text: Strychnine blocks glycine receptors in the spinal cord. Glycine normally inhibits muscle contraction.

twist.text: Without inhibition, every muscle fires at once. The body arches backward in a bridge—called opisthotonus.

climax.text: Agatha Christie used strychnine in her first novel. She knew the chemistry from working in a pharmacy.

punchline.text: Block the off-switch for muscles. Everything contracts at once.

quiz.question: How does strychnine cause death?
options: It blocks glycine receptors, removing inhibition of muscle contraction
It prevents oxygen from binding to hemoglobin

details.summary: Strychnine is an alkaloid from the Strychnos nux-vomica tree that blocks glycine receptors in the spinal cord, causing uncontrolled muscle spasms and a horrifically painful death through exhaustion and asphyxiation while the victim remains fully conscious.
details.whyItMatters: Strychnine's dramatic symptoms made it prominent in both murder cases and detective fiction. Its mechanism of action advanced understanding of inhibitory neurotransmitter pathways in the nervous system.
takeaways: Strychnine blocks inhibitory glycine receptors in the spinal cord
Victims experience violent convulsions while remaining conscious
Agatha Christie featured strychnine in her first novel

faq.question: Why does strychnine cause such violent muscle spasms?
faq.answer: Normally, glycine inhibits motor neurons to prevent excessive contraction. Strychnine blocks these glycine receptors, removing the braking system on muscle activation. Without inhibition, every sensory input triggers maximum muscle contraction simultaneously.

faq.question: Is strychnine still used for any legitimate purposes today?
faq.answer: Strychnine has been largely eliminated from commercial products. It was historically used as rat poison and in small doses as a stimulant tonic. Some countries still use it for pest control in restricted agricultural settings, though safer alternatives are now preferred.
